utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution I'm Tom Hannis. Along with me today is our intern, Ms. Taisier Adil, and my case manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Isabel Düsterhöft for -- appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Aleksandar Aleksic, Miroslav Cuskic, Gillian Kelly, and Milena Dzudovic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Aleksandar Lazarevic for Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Kovac. As the Chamber moves into its final set of questions for you before it turns over to the counsel for either side, I remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovac. Mr. Kovac, yesterday you told us how you personally had to deal with people to be disciplined or removed from the service. You mentioned in particular the proceedings against Stevan Todorovic, Simo Drljaca, and Dragan Andan. Now, my question to you is: According to you, did -- in 1992, did the minister at the time, Mico Stanisic, enjoy the authority and have the same responsibility to remove these persons, the ones you named and we discussed, to remove them from service and initiate appropriate proceedings against them?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had that authority and he indeed did that through me and the institutions that I headed. We were a team, in other words. At the Ministry of the Interior, the assistant minister cannot possibly want to do some things that the minister does not want to be done. That was obvious while Mr. Adzic was minister and wanted to do some things that were contrary to the wishes of us professionals. I understood it to be Mr. Stanisic's wish to do the things that I was doing. And it follows from some documents that Minister Stanisic was involved in some proceedings, except in the case of Todorovic. Yesterday there was something of a mix-up. One document refers to the time when I took measures and two other measures have to do with Adzic and Kijac. But the one document that has to do with the time while I was in office certainly shows the co-ordination of the various bodies of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now then, still on that authority to discipline and to remove eventually members of the force, I remember your opinion about Mr. Zupljanin as chief of the Banja Luka CSB and how things functioned over there. So I was wondering who had in principle and in practice the authority to discipline and to remove a chief of CSB, if need be? Who would have that authority in the first instance and who would have that in appeal?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first instance, the centre chief had that authority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But if it is about the centre chief himself, who would have the authority then?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister of the interior had authority over him. According to the later organisation, well, I'm now referring to the time when I was appointed, but at that time the chief of public security at the Ministry of the Interior also had such authority. In other words, when I took over public security, the centre chiefs were directly subordinated to the chief of public security who was also assistant minister, that is, assistant minister for public security. At any rate, the centre chiefs were certainly also under the jurisdiction of the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Now then in -- despite of your -- so you -- it's the -- on -- the responsibility and the authority is on the ministerial level, and you had a very particular opinion about the way the chief of centre in Banja Luka functioned. You didn't think it was necessary to take action then, against the chief at that time?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 we were going through the processes of setting up communication through administrations and by way of audits in the Banja Luka centre. The Banja Luka centre was differently structured than later. According to the then organisation, the Banja Luka centre had both a public security and a state security branch; and later on, when state security was separate from public security, we had centre chiefs for public security. My opinion of Zupljanin - and now I'm referring first and foremost to 1993 - was determined by his power to manage the centre. My basic criticism of the centre was about their organisational capability to keep the centre under control. I'm not saying that I had knowledge of Zupljanin taking part in some criminal activities or supporting sloppiness at the centre. I'm exclusively talking about an attitude that they in that region did not understand and they were resisting the centralisation of the ministry. They did not understand that such an organisation was the only option for us to counter the very complex situation on the ground, a situation that existed not only in Krajina but in the entire Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovac, can I remind you, your interview in 2003 at page 202 in the English version. I don't have the reference to the B/C/S version. It would be 227 or 228. Where you said that Stojan Zupljanin needed to be dismissed, and when that was done, it opened doors to the proceedings against other people.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but again I cannot ... Things are actually simple. At the time I only didn't explain. Replace Zupljanin at the time meant give rise to an unofficial existence of an SAO Krajina and the minister of the interior. That was the reality of the time. I don't know if you'll understand, though. It was my opinion that removing Stojan Zupljanin and replacing him by staff who were exclusively loyal to the MUP headquarters would enable us to access more directly public security stations, which Stojan Zupljanin lacked the power to do so. But eventually it turned out that we were not strong enough either because the centres were too strong. We were striving to centralise the entire police structure in the Krajina. I don't know if I need to clarify additionally. I can provide you with the causalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at page 200 in your October 2003 interview you referred to a dispatch by Mico Stanisic in August 1992, asking for courts to be formed and criminals to be tried. When was this dispatch sent and to whom was it sent? Who was to set up these courts?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me that the English and Serbian pages don't match. I cannot see this in the Serbian version and I also think it doesn't match the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have in front of me is about Zvornik, my statements about Zvornik and the paramilitaries there. I can answer your question, but what I see here isn't about any kind of dispatch. I see the section where I speak about our tackling the issue of the paramilitaries in Zvornik, Zuco, Cuko, and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I quote from page 200, at the bottom of 200. "And we from the MUP," you declared, "were the first ones who had the guts to send the dispatch in which Stanisic demanded the courts to be formed, that the criminals, the perpetrators, are to be tried." You remember this; and if so, can you tell me to whom the dispatch was sent and when it was sent?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. But still, I don't understand why I cannot see what you read out in Serbian. I can see it's there in English and I partly understand it, but I can't see it in the Serbian. But ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have the correct page in Serbian. Mr. Zecevic, could you be of assistance? Or Mr. Aleksic, whoever. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's the right page in Serbian. The paragraph in question is the top paragraph. It can be enlarged if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, I --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it now. Yes, I have it now. I cannot remember the details of that dispatch because it's been 20 years. But I know of a dispatch by which it was demanded that other bodies, apart from MUP bodies, be set up faster so that all proceedings against all persons, all perpetrators of crimes, can be started in accordance with the law. Because in some areas the problem was that there were no organised institutions that could take over and process persons from the Ministry of the Interior. I'm, first of all, referring to prosecutor's offices and courts. There was an institutional vacuum. There was no legal vacuum, though --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, we know the context. We would like to know, if you can tell us, to whom this request was sent: Please organise the courts so that perpetrators can be prosecuted. To whom was it sent? Who was supposed to put that in place?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, the relevant ministries, like the Ministry of Justice. But also regional organs that were already in place, the regional courts could contribute as well who hadn't exactly been developed up to the local level, and I know that there was such an attempt both in the ministry and the regional centres where these institutions existed. However, they did not exist at lower levels. And I also think that many military units that were joining the VRS definitely didn't have a fully developed system of military courts and judiciary, and this caused the problems of how to treat the people who committed crimes or members of the military involved in any illegal activities. There was, as I said, no legal vacuum, but we did have an organisational vacuum at the lowest level and that was a priority for us, in view of the fact that there were terrible devastations and destruction and we were short staffed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at tab 13, P408. And can we have page 2. And could you read what is said there about the municipality of Samac at -- it's at the bottom of the English version of page 2. It's about Samac and Doboj high court.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The courts and the prosecutor's office in the Serbian municipality in Samac were not operational; that was the information that we had. And this exactly confirms what I said a minute ago to the effect that the prosecutor's offices and courts had not been set up in Samac, but that cases had to be referred to Doboj. So this is a true reflection of the actual situation. It demonstrates that in the municipalities where the crime rate was the most serious, the fully-fledged institutional foundations were not set up for prosecuting certain persons and for identifying the perpetrators and impose sanctions. So we have an institutional vacuum here, as was the situation in Samac. So we at the ministry were the first one to pin-point these problems, and we requested the relevant organs and structures in the political sphere as well to have an institutional system in place and we see that the regional centre in Doboj took over the prosecutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is some inconsistency here whether there was no will to do that, but anyway we were facing these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So Doboj courts were functioning. Now, can we turn over to the next page in English. In the second paragraph it refers to crimes of thefts -- of thefts and aggravated theft. And I was wondering were other crimes such as those encumbered or such as those committed in detention centres not investigated and referred to the prosecutor's office, whether it would be civilian or the military prosecutor? This seems only to be about theft and aggravated theft but not about the other serious crimes that were committed at that time. Is there, in your view, any particular reason for that, why those other crimes were not prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the situation in Samac, it only makes sense to me that they would start with recording these minor offences and without any serious attempts to remove the people who committed more serious crimes. At this initial period this was probably the best that they could do on the ground, the people who investigated the crimes in view of the professional capabilities of Saric and another person because at that time that was the maximum that they could do to reach those levels. So as I said, this was an initial stage of dealing with criminality in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kovac. That is all I had for you as questions. I want to apologise to the parties for the extension of time it took to examine Mr. Kovac in chief. I have a few mitigating factors or circumstances to that, of which one is that this is the very first time that I do this kind of exercise. So I'm learning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours. It's pretty good for a first time, Your Honour, and I'm glad to see you suffer some of the same problems that we've had for two years. We feel your pain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I'd like to start with something that was touched on this morning by Judge Delvoie concerning Mr. Zupljanin and your opinion about him. I think at page 4 this morning of the transcript - let me get it precisely - line 12 you said: "My opinion of Zupljanin - and now I'm referring first and foremost to 1993 - was determined by his power to manage the centre. And my basic criticism was about their organisational capability to keep the centre under control." Now, I take it then you did not form that opinion until 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had an opinion on that issue prior to 1993, already at the end of 1992 or actually from the very beginning of 1993 I entertained such an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, we've seen evidence and we've heard from some witnesses that suggest that CSB Banja Luka and Mr. Zupljanin in 1992 were held generally in high regard and that his CSB was probably the best one working in 1992 in the RS MUP. Would you not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, the Banja Luka CSB was the only one among the centres in addition to Doboj who maintained their HQ location. They were not relocated, as was the case with other centres. But there's another thing here: The right of each leadership, including myself who was tasked with establishing public security service, to make my own assessment in that respect and to set up the central MUP, the central institutions, and the central management. Now, when we speak about the Krajina and the relations between the Krajina and the centre and Pale, has been a conflicting one to this day. So Banja Luka wanted to have the central MUP all the time and they were happy only when that happened in 1997 and 1998. So the residual elements of the SAO Krajina were very much present, both in the police and the army. So, to put it simply, in that area we had very much resistance to the institutions, without which we thought it was impossible to establish a proper system that would be suitable to a war time. So we couldn't have SAO Krajinas and other small municipalities or principalities if we were to combat all the difficulties that we faced. So this was the root of all the problems that we encountered. And then, as a result of that, in 1993 control was lost over CSB, both physically and operationally, and as a consequence we from the central MUP had to put this under control, arrest the people who were responsible and bring some order. I think that this is a sufficient explanation as to why I thought about their capabilities in that area the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me stop you there. Yesterday the Judge indicated to you that we have limited time and we hope to get you out of here by the end of Friday. So I'll ask you to try and focus on my question and if it calls for a simple answer, try and give me a short, simple answer. My question was: Would you agree with that? A yes or no would have done for a starter and then we could have gone on. Now, Mr. Zupljanin had been appointed as chief of the CSB for Banja Luka by Minister Stanisic, correct, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly. I think that before that he was appointed to that position by Alija Delimustafic. Before Stanisic appointed him, he was the centre of the chief [as interpreted] while Delimustafic was in office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to tab 124 on the Prosecution's list. In e-court the English page I want to look at first is at page 14 going on to page 15, and the B/C/S is at page 9. And I've got a hard copy. If the usher would assist me, I'll hand that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, coming your way is a document dated the 22nd of June, 1992. It's a decision from Minister Stanisic appointing Stojan Zupljanin as chief of the Banja Luka security services centre in your Ministry of the Interior. Have you ever seen that before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was no need for me to look at it. I'm sure that it's an authentic document, but I would just like to say once again that this man was at the head of the Banja Luka CSB while the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina was still operational. So there is a continuity there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a continuity by choice of Minister Stanisic; right? He didn't have to keep him on. He could have appointed somebody else; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that period, the way we operated was to have the personnel in certain positions, provided they accepted to continue to work, Stanisic would confirm their appointments. He had the right not to appoint people, but the majority of the staff had been originally appointed by him and I thought -- I think that in war time he didn't have much choice to look for other staff. And I don't think anything disputable about Zupljanin's appointment at that time - particularly in view of what he's been charged here. The only objection we had at the time was that he was much too loyal to Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in what way did he manifest that loyalty to Delimustafic in April, May, June of 1992? Can you give us an example or show us a document?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there was a dispatch in that Zupljanin said after the referendum at least, well, that's what Banja Luka was saying, that he was going to perform his tasks. As far as I am concerned, I was the SJB chief and this was not a criticism of Stanisic's attitude. It was rather perceived as a process and as a continuity of the chiefs who had originally been appointed by Delimustafic and then the Serbian MUP just accepted and adopted this continuity. So nothing special about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in Prijedor, the SJB chief at the time the war began was Haris Talundzic, a Muslim. He wasn't kept on in the RS MUP as the SJB chief in Prijedor, was he? Because Simo Drljaca was appointed an SJB chief. So no continuity in Prijedor; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about Prijedor. I was the chief of the public security station in Ilidza. Therefore, I cannot make any comments relating to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were able to make the comment about CSB Banja Luka; right? Okay. Let me ask you then about something you said yesterday at page 27071. You were speaking with Judge Delvoie and you said -- you were talking about the rebellion in September of 1993 in Banja Luka, with the CSB Banja Luka centre being thrown over as a result of this army rebellion. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understood you to be saying that's when you really became convinced that Mr. Zupljanin wasn't capable of controlling a centre, and therefore he ought to be removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, that was the ultimate reason and it was impossible to go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at -- tab 124 is, I think, 65 ter number 20061, and I'd like to look at another page. The English in e-court is page 16 going on 17, and the B/C/S is page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'll hand you a hard copy of this document, with the assistance of the usher. This is dated 16 October 1993, so sometime after the rebellion we're talking about. You'll see at the bottom it appears to be your name and you're listed as the minister of the interior, Tomislav Kovac. Is that correct on the 16th of October, 1993? It's a decision appointing Stojan --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot -- I cannot make any statement about this because there's no signature of mine. I know that in another CSB headed by Brane Pecanac there was a group, but I was all the time in Banja Luka working as an acting minister of the interior because in that period practically nobody was at the head of the Banja Luka CSB. First of all, on the 16th of October, 1993, I was an acting minister, and that's how it should be stated, not "Minister Tomislav Kovac." Therefore, I cannot authenticate this document --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so I must tell you that I never signed such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. On the 16th of October, Ratko Adzic was no longer the minister of the interior, he had left; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did leave, but based on a decree I was appointed acting minister. I wasn't appointed to that post because I hadn't gone through the proper procedure in the Assembly that pertained to all ministers. Because there was an imminent threat of war, I was appointed acting minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. And there was no one else in the ministry above you at that time, in October 1993; right? You were the highest authority in the ministry in October 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you saying this document wasn't issued by the ministry appointing Stojan Zupljanin as chief of the CSB in October 1993, or you just don't remember whether you signed one?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that I didn't sign this document and that at the time it should have read "acting minister Tomislav Kovac." I'm telling you that the factual situation was such that there was no need for such a decision to be issued because a special working group was set up to run the centre. At the time the group led by Pecanac. This group worked all the way through January 1994 when Minister Stanisic came and issued letters of appointment for the regular leadership of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And what actions, if any, did you personally take in 1993 to try and remove Mr. Zupljanin, given your opinion of his work? Did you do anything as acting minister?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated this several times quite clearly. In September 1993, when the military forces occupied the CSB and the Banja Luka SJB, this practically spelled the suspension of the operation of the Banja Luka CSB physically, factually, and operationally. So this institution was occupied and there was no functioning of MUP services. In view of such extraordinary circumstances and after arresting the rebels, when we entered the premises we simply took them over and that was followed by assessing up of a commission that was to run the CSB Banja Luka. So in actual fact we had a situation in which previously Zupljanin and his group had been removed by coup d'etats as it were. And in order to rectify this situation, which was very grave, we simply appointed in group led by Brane Pecanac who until that time was a special unit commander, which only demonstrates what kind of personnel we had to appoint to these position --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. In 1994, when Mr. Stanisic came back for his second term as a minister, did he discuss with you that one of his primary goals was to try and do something about the crimes that had happened in late August at Mount Vlasic, Koricanske Stijene, where 150 -- somewhere between 150 and 200 Muslims had been taken off the bus, lined up along the edge of the cliff, and machine-gunned. You knew about that crime; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out subsequently. I got information from groups that went there on behalf of the ministry to deal with that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you first learned about it in 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot state with certainty when exactly I heard it for the first time, but I was not involved in any actions taken by the ministry with regard to that and therefore cannot comment on the exact time when I learned about it. The chief of crime enforcement at the time, Goran Macar, was in charge of the activities taken at the time; that much I know. But I couldn't give you any additional details.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, though, in 1994, when Mr. Stanisic came back for his second term as minister, did he not inform you that this was a priority for him and he wanted to try to get to the bottom of that because there was good evidence that it had been committed by members of the police or the intervention platoon from Prijedor. You remember him telling you about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no reason for him to give me these specifics. When Stanisic returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he clearly insisted on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please stop. I just asked if you remember him telling you about that. You told me no. That's all I need. And regarding Mr. Zupljanin after the coup d'etat, did you take any steps to make sure that Mr. Zupljanin didn't return to Banja Luka to act as the chief there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any special need to take particular steps. He wasn't an enemy of the state. I -- it was my assessment that I could go through the commission of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me jump back in time to the beginning of your career. You've had quite a career in the police. I think you told us that you started out in the state security side of the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you told us that after a series of successful tasks, in 1984 you were appointed chief inspector for state security. That's a pretty high position and by my calculations at that time you were 25 years old, is that right? 1984?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mention you worked in the covert operations department, that means spy work basically; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, tell me what it does mean.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, secret surveillance, secret arrests, when I say "secret," that's to be understood conditionally. But it's no longer secret now so I can tell you about it if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, but the point I'm trying to get at, the nature of that work involves sometimes being able to represent yourself as someone you're not, pretending to be someone else, giving misinformation to other people as part of your investigations to see who's talking to whom, who's passing or leaking information, et cetera. Is that one of the things that you do in the secret police?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was a police member who had particular mental and physical abilities, and I took part in arrests and in the seizing of documents of Alija Izetbegovic and Vojislav Seselj and some other terrorists who were preparing to launch terrorist actions during the Olympic Games in Sarajevo. Those were my results [as interpreted] why I was promoted at such young an age. And what you are talking about, yes, I made use of such people as an operative worker. They were our co-workers, we worked with them, but they weren't members of state security. They were hired guns, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. The actual work you yourself did, though, included sometimes arresting and interrogating individuals; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People are arrested to be interrogated. Of course we did that. The -- those people were a threat to the constitutional order as it existed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And sometimes during interrogations hands were put on those being interrogated; right? Sometimes you used physical means during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the time we were a rather advanced service. We used methods like those used in Western democracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are talking about specific physical activity, I can describe you a specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me stop you. I'm just saying in regard to your answer, I can tell you in Western democracies that police sometimes have been known to put hands on suspects during interrogations, hands, telephone books, feet. You understand what I'm talking about, don't you? And, Mr. Kovac, there's no great shame in that because, as far as I can tell, it happens in all police in all the world. Are you saying that that didn't happen in your police, either before or during the war? Is that what you're saying under oath?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's a misunderstanding. I worked on such jobs. I used my physical force to overpower terrorists and prevent them from murdering people; that's -- that was my claim to fame. The work of state security is different from public security when it comes to interrogating criminals by making use of phone directories. Our job is particular, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying, to your knowledge, in 1992, from April through December, in the RS MUP physical force wasn't used during interrogation of detained non-Serbs? You know that happened, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, certainly. But let me remind you, since you have mentioned my file. Up until the war I was chairman of the disciplinary board for the Sarajevo region, and I was known for sanctioning members for much lesser offences. And you probably know that people are appointed to such positions who have -- who meet certain standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned at page 27034 yesterday that when you got appointed by Mr. Stanisic to be assistant minister for police tasks and affairs, that later on he gave you that authorisation to act for him in his absence. You said: "The post of deputy minister did not exist." I want to ask you, though, didn't Momcilo Mandic hold the post and sign documents as deputy minister of the new Serb MUP in April and May of 1992? Do you know anything about that? Before he went over to be minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that there was no post of deputy minister. Momcilo Mandic was probably appointed by the government or maybe the Assembly to that position. Stanisic skillfully circumvented my appointment because he knew that I didn't stand a chance for political reasons, at least that's my view. So he wanted to avoid going through the process of getting political approval for my appointment. That's my interpretation anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Makes sense. Thank you. You were talking to Judge Delvoie yesterday about Exhibit P163, which are the minutes of a collegium meeting on the 20th of August in Trebinje. Do you remember that meeting? It was probably the first one that you went to once you were on that level.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the participants in this meeting were talking about the problems they had in their area and that there was a process going on to eradicate the flaws within the MUP, as you describe it. You say: "The second part of my involvement was my suggestion to Mr. Stanisic to tackle the matter of decision-makers because the existing personnel were unable to do that. We needed a more efficient and more decisive people from the level of the ministry all the way down to police stations. So there was no doubt as to what to do with these people." When you say "there was no doubt about what to do with these people," are you talking about the indecisive ones in the existing personnel? Is that who you meant?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document here, but I'll answer you anyway. I certainly was referring to indecisive people; incompetent people; people who were under the influence of local structures and local politics; and clearly, by extension, to people who couldn't continue due to their criminal activity. And that attitude of mine also determined my programme when it comes to the severity of measures to be taken in the management process in order to tackle all these problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Do you -- can you tell me by name any people that fit into that description of the indecisive ones that had to be replaced on the ministry level, any assistant ministers that you put in that category in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanisic had already completed the changes, he had already appointed assistant ministers and chiefs of administrations; that was done. I was assistant for the police, Macar was in charge of crime, Dragan Kijac of state security, so the personnel roster was already completed. As for the lower structures, there wasn't much left to remove because the order of the day was to create institutions. That was my task in Bijeljina, create administrations that will supervise the work of the ministry in order -- or rather, in accordance with the laws and regulations. We didn't have a central MUP, it stayed behind on the Bosniak side, and we had to build the structures of our MUP institutionally and personnel-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next document that -- well, the next topic that Judge Delvoie asked you about was your relationship with Mr. Stanisic in 1992 [Realtime transcript read in error "1982"] and then later when he came back. At page 27050 you said: "Well, we're different personalities. I wouldn't say we were on exactly good terms. We were professionally on good terms. During his second term of office there appeared some disagreements." So what had changed between 1992 and 1994 that led to you having some disagreements and what were those disagreements about, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention in the transcript, 23, 3, it says "1982." I believe Mr. Hannis said "1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I certainly meant to say "1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, that was just to clear up the transcript. Do you remember my question or should I ask it again?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember your question. You asked me what changed in 1994 in the relationship between me and Stanisic. That was your question; right? Nothing special changed except that Stanisic, when he returned for his second term in office, at least to my understanding, he wanted to replace some people in managing positions due to criminal activities and he wanted to defeat them politically. I don't think that it was a realistic assessment on his part, and subsequently it became clear that the MUP would suffer a new blow. This was the difference between us. And after one year Stanisic was removed again. The forces he stood up against were stronger and I remained in my position for another year. I think it -- that year made a difference because I made a contribution. But after that one additional year, I was replaced according to the same scenario as he.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. One question for the transcript. Witness mentioned specific name and it's not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you heard what Mr. Krgovic said. Did you mention any specific names as -- and I take it that was referring to the people that he wanted to defeat? In your answer did you mention some specific names; and if so, in what context?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Momcilo Krajisnik, the speaker of the Assembly of the RS. I thought I was being clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It wasn't picked up in the transcript, that's why we followed-up. One more short topic before the break. You were asked about the letter that you wrote I think three days after you came up to the ministry, the one that was sent to the president and to the prime minister about the need to categorise people who were detained. You remember that? I can show it to you, but I think you remember that letter pretty well?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And Judge Delvoie asked why did you send it to the prime minister and the president instead of addressing it to your boss, Mr. Stanisic? You said: "There was no need for me to communicate with Stanisic because we managed to agree on many things." And then you said: "I saw it as a reflection of the task that we had in Trebinje ..." But that can't be right because your letter was written on the 9th of August, 11 days before the meeting in Trebinje. So can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe there was a mistake. The process that started before Trebinje, and continued after Trebinje, went in that very direction. All my contacts -- and as soon as I arrived at the ministry HQ, I explained to Mr. Stanisic what the direction of action was and what we must tackle, so that in essence there is no difference really. It's a result of the activities from the very first day since I arrived. And I clearly stated what was my intention as soon as I arrived at the ministry. We constantly dealt with these matters from the first moment on, and all this is a result of our talks and the directions of action that we had agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With Their Honours' permission we'll take our first break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, before the witness came in I just wanted to raise one thing. This is only the second time I think in 10 or 11 years here I've been in court in a situation where a witness has a lawyer with him or appointed for him for the purposes of the testimony. But I'm not sure how that interacts with our general admonition to witnesses that they aren't supposed to talk about their testimony with anybody, you know, during the recess or at the end of the day. Now, I don't know what Your Honours' position is and I -- it just occurred to me and I thought I would bring it to your attention, whether or not you feel there's any need to make an instruction or direction to counsel or to the witness, I would ask you to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, in my view such an instruction was already issued by the Trial Chamber yesterday after we finished with Mr. Kovac's testimony, and he was instructed not to be approached by anyone but his counsel. This is in my view sufficient instruction, and I did approach and I do spend these short breaks with Mr. Kovac. I see really no need for this sort of intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I thank both Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Hannis for their observations, and of course the -- from Mr. Lazarevic's response, he has indicated an awareness of the -- that balance which he has to strike in terms of -- because, Mr. Hannis, you would be aware of the reason why the Chamber agreed to the appointment of Mr. Lazarevic to assist -- I shouldn't say to assist, to protect the interests of Mr. -- of the witness who's -- the content of whose testimony is finely drawn but could easily shade into matters which involve -- which would invoke Rule -- the provisions of Rule 90(E). So Mr. Lazarevic from his own -- what he himself has stated is aware of the -- that distinction between not - for want of a better word - contaminating the witness's testimony before the Chamber and ensuring that the witness's interests are thus protected. And unless there is nothing further, we would have the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just would add this, and it's not -- this is not anything pertaining to Mr. Lazarevic because I've only had good experiences with him. But in -- I think in the other situation I was involved in, what the Judge had done was allowed the lawyer to sit in the courtroom and if the witness needed or wanted to consult with him during the proceedings, he did so. But we all knew when that happened, and then they were directed not to have any contact outside the courtroom. But I don't know if that's necessary or desirable, but I only bring it to your attention as to what was done in one other case to my knowledge. Because it's only a matter of appearances, you understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, your experience, of course, is more extensive than mine in this regard, and the one other case with which I'm familiar, counsel in the position of Mr. Lazarevic actually sat next -- immediately -- right next to the witness on the stand, so the -- but we'll see, yes. So could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I will return to your August 9th letter, but I wanted to talk about a different topic right now. And this relates to award nominations. I'd like to show you Exhibit Number P648. This is at tab 101 of the Prosecution's binder, and I have a hard copy for you. This document is dated the 20th of September, 1993, and you'll see it's from Tihomir Glavas, listed as a chief of the public security station in Ilidza, your old station. You knew Mr. Glavas; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he a good policeman, an honest policeman?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a good policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you've seen this document before during one of your interviews with representatives from my office, the OTP. Do you recall it now that you're looking at it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not much. I'm trying to refresh my memory by reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you don't mind, I'd like to go to some particular paragraphs and ask you about those, and if you feel like you need to read the rest of it to answer my question, then indicate to me at the time. But if you can address it right now, I'll try to proceed in that fashion. And the first one I wanted to ask you about is on page 2 in both the English and the B/C/S. Fortunately, this is a document where the page breaks are the same. And it's in the middle of the page, the paragraph reads in English as: "At the beginning of 1991, during illegal meetings organised by Kovac, Tomislav, commander of the Ilidza public security station at the time, policemen of Serbian nationality were informed that the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted and it was agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality." Is that correct? Is that true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is inaccurate, and therefore it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what way is it not true? Did you not organise meetings with the policemen of Serbian nationality?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. Probably they as the security centre did make some reviews, but I was posted at Ilidza and all my activities were strictly relating to Ilidza and the quoting all these places makes no sense. Let me just remind you that in 1991, when I was the president of the disciplinary court, I tried Malko Koroman from Pale because there was suspicion --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, please, please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, you don't. That wasn't my question. Would you wait.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So are you saying you didn't organise meetings with policemen of the Serbian nationality to talk about the war option being increasingly promoted, not just by the Serb side but by all three sides? Did you not organise meetings with the Serbian policemen?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no possibility to do that according to this document because this encompasses a wider area and I restricted myself to Ilidza alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did you organise meetings of Serbian policemen at the Ilidza public security station? Did you organise meetings of policemen from the Ilidza public security station?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need for that. I had a reserve police force and I communicated with them daily within the scope of regular activities; therefore, there was no need for an unlawful activities to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it the only -- the only word you disagree with then is "illegal"?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with the entire statement and the entire paragraph or whatever you call it. All I can say is that this is not true. And if you're asking me about some other things that are not mentioned here, I already told you that in the area of the Ilidza SJB where I was commander, I had direct contacts with reserve police force and active-duty policemen. And if you want me to speak about that, I can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about did you have meetings with only Serb policemen from Ilidza public security station to talk about the situation? Were there only Serbs in your component, no non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about early 1992, before April?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before April, or rather, from March onwards when a division took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina between the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats, organisation was being undertaken at the level of local communes, and it did not pertain only to police stations. Other ethnic communities did the same and they organised themselves in the very same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. You are telling us that you weren't involved in arming the Serb population in late 1991 and early 1992 before the war; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by the beginning of the war. For us the war started --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when the first activities -- I don't know what you mean by this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Before April 6th. In late 1991 and before April 6th, 1992, were you involved in arming the Serb population in the area of Ilidza public security station, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a clear answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A yes -- yes or no would be a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- in March when the Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, can you not answer it yes or no? That would be a clear answer, one of those two words.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. The way you're putting this question is not proper. Because in my area the war started --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop, stop. Sir, you're a witness. Your job here is to answer questions that are put to you. If I ask an inappropriate question, your lawyer or one of those lawyers over there can make an objection to the Judge and then they can tell me, "No, Mr. Hannis, you can't ask it that way." But in the absence of an objection, I've asked you a question and your role here is to answer it the best you can. And my question called for a yes or no answer. Can you answer that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war started before the date that you are citing in my area and I can only speak in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm only asking you between late 1991, let's say September 1991 through April 6, 1992 - whatever date you say the war started - during that time did you involve yourself in arming the Serb population in the area of the Ilidza public security station, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March when the Muslim forces attempted to take over the republic depots that were situated in my area, I blocked these depots and that is how we got hold of those weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And actually, the Muslims had been trying to arm themselves even before that date, right, as far as back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hannis. Maybe there's an intermediate question to the witness, namely, when you got hold of those weapons, what did you do with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those weapons belonged to the republican staff of the Territorial Defence. The Green Berets, with the assistance of the then assistant minister of the interior Selimovic, were very much engaged in retrieving the weapons from these weapons [as interpreted]. The Crisis Staff of Ilidza decided that this area has to be cordoned off. We blocked the depot, and from that, the Crisis Staff of Ilidza took over the depot and distributed the weapons according to its existing organisation, military organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this had been a concern for some time before March -- March 5. It had been a concern for you for some time before that date, right, because you saw the Muslims and the Green Berets trying to organise by increasing the reserve police force and arming Muslims in your area as far back as late 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before I continue on in that document I want to show you something else to see if that might refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is tab 111, Your Honours, it's Exhibit P841.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I'll hand you a hard copy of this, with assistance from the usher. This is from March 1st, 1996, and it purports to be an interview by you given to a woman named Gordana Jovanovic with a publication called "Interview." I think it was associated with "Borba." And I believe you were also shown this document during one of your interviews with the OTP. Do you remember seeing it before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was shown to me by the OTP, but I do remember this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you remember giving this interview?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you ever read it before?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it was published in the magazine "Interview," that's when I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time did you find any inaccuracies or untruths in it that you felt you needed to bring to the attention of the author, or did you find it to be accurate?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think that everything was exactly correct. There were some mistakes, but the interview was already published, and the practice of this periodical was not the one that required authentication prior to publishing. Therefore, there were some untruthful statements but not too many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever bring any of those untruthful statements to the attention of the author or anybody at the OTP or anyone else? Or were they minor enough that you didn't bother?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the OTP because I never discussed this topic with the OTP. I don't remember discussing it with them and I don't think there were any particular objections. Already at that time I was not minister any longer. This was an unofficial interview and it's only to be expected that there could be some inaccuracies, both on the part of the journalist and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I certainly understand that based on my experience with some journalists. Could you look at page 2 of your B/C/S copy, and in English we need to go to page 4. For you, Mr. Kovac, it's in the right-hand column under that big heading about General Kukanjac's guilt and then a smaller heading about "Let's go back to Sarajevo and the beginnings of the war conflicts ..." And it's the second paragraph near the bottom of that paragraph. You'll see a reference to 4.000 barrels. And below that I'm reading. It says: "As far as I'm concerned there were no major battles in Ilidza, at least not in the beginning. For a year there, I did everything that the Muslims were doing. They were strengthening the reserve force, so was I. They were arming themselves, I did not lag behind. I saw that they were forming some paramilitary units, I did the same." That's correct, isn't it? That's what you were doing in Ilidza in late 1991 and/or early 1992, before April?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please give me a little so that I can get to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I say that I saw that they were forming some paramilitary formations, I didn't have the need to do so. I had my reserve police force and I was primarily referring to them in terms of strengthening the existing organisation. Therefore, I didn't set up any paramilitary units because there was no necessity for that. I was probably referring to the reserve police force. The chief Mlivic and I decided that the reserve police would be under his jurisdiction and the majority Serb entities would be under my command, and this is the agreement we had reached in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But what about the part where you said the Muslims were strengthening the reserves, so I take it that you were strengthening your reserve force, and you were arming, you did not lag far behind the Muslims who were arming themselves. So you were arming the Serbs as well, right? That's what it says. That's what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason because I know exactly when the Muslim forces started arming themselves, and the main agreement with the Patriotic League was reached in Hrasnica. I knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- very well about what was happening --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, please, stop --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- please, you're not answering my question. Is that what you did or not?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of March, following the occupation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us about that --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a depot --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You already told us about --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is exactly what I had in mind when I gave this interview as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you were lagging pretty far behind the Muslims then if you didn't start arming the Serbs until the 5th of March, right, because they had been doing it for some months before; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately we were very much naive and, as a consequence, we were lagging behind in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But that's not what you told the reporter. You said you didn't lag far behind. And yesterday when you were talking about your letter on the 9th of August about categorising prisoners, you noticed that even though you'd only been on the job three days you'd done that because you described yourself as a speedy individual who likes to get things done quickly. It seems to me you would have liked to have gotten yourself armed and your reserve force beefed up quickly when you saw the Muslims were doing that. Come on now, that's what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a schoolboy to admit something or not admit something. At the time, members of the Serb ethnicity responded en masse to the call-up of the JNA and they entered the barracks in our area, specifically Lukavica, and they took over all the most lethal weapons like tanks, rocket-launchers, et cetera. On the other hand, Alija Izetbegovic prevented Muslims from going to the army and they seized the assets of the JNA. And that was the substance and the essence of the arming of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everything else, speaking about rifles, TO weapons, outdated weapons, is something that forced the Serbs to take over only as a result of erroneous decisions taken by Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that they got hold of was only the result of their response to the call-up from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not -- I wasn't asking you whether this was being done in self-defence or for some other reason. I was only asking you if you did that. I guess my next question: Do you remember saying that to the reporter? That's what you told her, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you something. When I spoke about the arming and the reserve force and being the -- an army officer, I can tell you what the truthful essence of the army of the Serb people is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo there were enormous assets belonging to the JNA and 80 per cent of the personnel --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, please, Mr. Kovac. Are you not getting a correct interpretation of my question? It was: Is that what you told the reporter, what we've been reading out there?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, you are changing the dimension. I spoke --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to this journalist and I told her about the disarming of the 5th of March --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Arming of the 5th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you how the arming of all the three peoples in Ilidza --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, please --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- looked like --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question and I don't have much time. I'm sorry, I'll move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go back to Mr. Glavas' recommendation, I think you have it under the newspaper story there. It's the other document on top of your binder. If you could go to page 3 and I think it's the fourth paragraph down in both English and B/C/S. And Mr. Glavas is writing. In the middle of that paragraph, he said: "Covering the communications system was always done in the presence of at least one Serb. All telegrams concerning important -- or containing important messages addressed to Mlivic, Edin, chief of the station, were first shown to Tomo Kovac and then they were acted upon according to the agreement." Is that correct? Is that what was happening? Some Serb who worked in communication department made sure you got to see all incoming documents before they went to the chief? That was a good way to keep an eye on what the Muslims were up to, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't like that. Through this form of communication they couldn't prepare anything in particular. There was a Muslim and a Serb always side by side. They probably wanted to earn for themselves some credits because it seems that this document speaks more about certain services trying to augment their role rather than to speak about what I did, because those were epic times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know what epic behaviour is when it comes to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Maybe we can talk about that after court, but I need to move on to the matters I'm limited to. You say that this isn't exactly right because they probably wanted to earn for themselves some credit. You mean Mr. Glavas is trying to earn some kind of credit for himself by writing this about what happened and about your role in it? How does that add to Mr. Glavas' status - I don't understand - to say that you, Tomo Kovac, were getting all the communications before they went to the chief? How does that make Mr. Glavas look any better to anybody? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, speaking about the people who were working at the communications centre, maybe it was them who wanted to look better than they did. So this was a fragmented statement. This speaks more about themselves but not about me or himself. So quite simply that was, as I said, epic times and people wanted to comment or praise themselves more than they wanted to praise me. I didn't need any praise because I had everything in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess we disagree on that because it does look like Mr. Glavas is praising you, and further evidence of that, if you could go to page 6 of that document. In the middle of the page: "Special credit goes to the following members of Ilidza public security station: "1. Kovac, Tomislav, commander, and later on chief of public security station. "He organised and was in charge of all above-mentioned activities. He gave special contribution in preparation of Serbian people for defence, formation of Serbian public security station, organisation of the illegal work, and arming of Serbian people." Is that not accurate? Or is he just laying it on thick again to make himself look better somehow?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the credit that I can claim was the fact that the Ilidza SJB was the only public security station in Sarajevo in which the commander managed to remain in his post. The Serbian personnel was expelled from all other public security stations around Sarajevo and probably this is why they think that this credit was due to me because I didn't allow anyone to move me from my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in answer to my question, is what he described you as having done true or not true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 5th of March, we take the depots and manage to arm the Serbian people, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry. There's no mention of the 5th of March in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No other dates are mentioned either.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right. So why are you mentioning a date? My question is: What it says here, you gave a special contribution in preparation of the Serbian people for defence, formation of the Serbian public security station, organisation of the illegal work, and arming of Serbian people. Is that true or not true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My particular contribution was the ability to stay in my position, whereas all other Serbian personnel was expelled from town. Only I stood my ground at the Ilidza station. That was my greatest contribution and this is this view. And I repeat, we were arming ourselves on the 5th of March and there were about 5- to 10.000 pieces of weapons in that depot and we took the depots, that's correct, and we distributed the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you go to the very last page, I think it's page 11, the very end, where you see Mr. Glavas' name or right above. One more, I think. On the back of that page you're looking at. At the bottom you see Mr. Glavas' name and right above that he said: "We suggest that Tomislav Kovac in accordance with the medal commission give his opinion for the type of reward for each individual." That sounds like you must have been consulted about this. Do you remember if you had seen this or you were consulted about the people that were proposed for medals, including yourself as number 1 in that list, or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember. This was absurd. Describing the good things that I did, they listed all these people too, that's what I said. And with regard to the positions in which these people were, this was a good basis for them to pass the commission. And of course, since I was at the head of the ministry, some sort of approval from me was required, although I didn't really have much time to deal with such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess my question is: Did you see it at the time and call up Mr. Glavas and say, "Hey, what you're writing about me is not correct and you're overdoing it, it's too much"? You didn't do that, did you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I put it to him like this. I think I said that by praising me they're actually praising themselves, but that's nothing all that special after all, especially given the circumstances at the time, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I will grant you that Mr. Glavas does actually list himself in there as one of the persons who should get an award, but he put you as number 1. The last name he puts on the list, I don't know if you see it right above his signature, the last person he recommended for an award was Sinisa Milic, and I believe that's the person that you and I probably know by the nickname Mongo; right? Sinisa Milic, isn't that the guy --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct, no. Sinisa Milic was the member of the special police unit who got killed. He was a member of a special police unit before the war and during the war he was killed in the -- in a traffic accident. He has nothing to do with Mongo. Mongo was a criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was Mongo's name?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Sinisa too, but he was a Sinisa Milic from Rakovica -- or rather, the Sinisa Milic from Rakovica was a police member, a different man, and he got killed in a traffic accident. He has nothing to do with Sinisa Mongo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, number 38 on the list is listed as Mongo; isn't that what it says? "Milic Sinisa - Mongo, Ilidza." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how come, but it was impossible for this one to be included because he was, after all, in conflict with the police. This is somebody's mistake. He couldn't possibly be on a list of our people. The other Milic who died in the accident was the one, whereas Sinisa Mongo was in conflict with the police and with me personally too. He tried to assassinate me two times, and eventually he overdosed and that's probably how he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We may speak about Mongo briefly a little later on. But I want to now go to the awards that actually culminated from this process. There are other recommendations from Miloje Kolarevic, from Branislav Okuka, and from somebody at the Blazoj reserve police station, but I don't think we have time for that. So if we could look at P732 at tab 106. This is a lengthy document, Mr. Kovac, so I need to give you a hard copy of that one as well, with help from the usher. And if you could give him back those two, I'll take them away from you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a list of awards and I believe that these were probably given out on Security Services Day in November of 1993, I don't remember if that's November 27th, something thereabouts. Do you recall receiving the Nemanjici commendation, Mr. Kovac? You're number 4 on the list here?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the only ones above you are the ministry itself, Mr. Stanisic, and Momcilo Mandic, who's listed as the former deputy minister. And I take it that's the highest award, right, that's higher than the next one down, the Karadjordjevic Star first class and second class and third class? Isn't that the highest award that was given?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the highest decoration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, there are other names on the list. On the next category of awards, first class Karadjordjevic Star, number 4 is Stojan Zupljanin and number 5 is Simo Drljaca. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's your opinion about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such was the opinion of their base and the ones who decided to award these decorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know who made that decision? Who was on the commission? Were those members of the MUP or was if from the SDS or from the government? Who was on the commission, if you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Colonel - what was his name? - former minister of defence, he was in charge of decorations all the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Bogdan Subotic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bogdan Subotic, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anybody else? He's from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was with the Ministry of Defence briefly and later he was in the office of the president of the republic, and it was from that position that he was involved. He may have been the president's advisor or some professional staff, but anyway a member of his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there were commissions who made proposals. Two levels of commissions, one from the basic body and then the state commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president's commission was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did anybody from MUP in 1993 during this process have any input on who got awards? I mean, was there any screening process where the acting minister or the minister or some high-level people in MUP headquarters got to review the list before the president actually issued the awards and say, "Oh, no, you shouldn't include number 7 because there's some problems with him"? Or was it simply -- well, do you know? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. As for these lower ranks, there were lists that originated from grass roots, and they were reviewed by the commissions. As for this highest decoration, decorations, the first two, they were in the jurisdiction of the state commission and the president of the republic. We could make proposals for the third level, but the highest two levels are in the exclusive jurisdiction of the president of the republic. There was such a rule book as far as I remember. At any rate, there was a procedure and there was a decree by which the president of the republic awards these decorations through his commissions. Maybe the Assembly was involved too and its bodies, but I'm not really all that familiar with the work of this awarding service. At that time, in 1993, decorations were the least of our worries in operational work. We had bigger fish to fry. But people -- some people liked this type of folklore and dealt with that, but we had much more serious work to do than this folklore, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]
