utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And other award recipients that you might be familiar with included Malko Koroman, Dusko Malovic, Ljuban Ecim, Mr. Glavas, and Stevo Todorovic from Bosanski Samac are all among award recipients. And I think you've given us some indication of your less-than-high opinion of some of those individuals. Did you have no connection or involvement with that process? For example, did you set up a committee to observe Security Services Day in 1993? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was a committee for the Security Services Day. There was some persons but not members of a commission. I know about this man Todorovic and some others who would never have gotten a decoration if anybody had asked me about it, but of course it wasn't up to me, it was up to the office of the president of the republic, and it was their right to decide who to decorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not MUP decorations. These are decorations given out by the president or -- those are state decorations, RS decorations. It was in their jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- we had commissions that could make proposals but -- what I want to say is that I absolutely was not involved in this because I had no time to deal with it --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- there were too many other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just going back to Mr. Glavas, before I showed you the document you told me he was a good policeman and an honest policeman. Why would he have said anything in that recommendation that wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I said that he was a solid policeman. I said that these documents are not really binding --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- these are proposals for decorations and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. You also agreed that he was an honest policeman, I thought, or are you saying something different?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he was a solid policeman and that the documents they submitted with the proposal are not binding. And the Serbs are like -- the Serbs like epic stuff, you know. They like to blow things up, embellish things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We've heard that. Let me show you 65 ter number 30044, I believe, it's tab 130 on the Prosecution list. I'll hand you a hard copy of this one with assistance from the usher. While it's coming to you, Mr. Kovac, I will tell you it's dated the 4th of November, 1993. And I think at this time you were acting minister of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this document is from you establishing an organisational committee to commemorate the day of security services. Do you remember that now?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that these markings are not my strong side. What it says here about the observing of the Security Services Day cannot be true because Security Services Day was in April, and in November this -- it's the MUP day or the MUP's patron saint's day. That may have been the matter here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I don't know to what extent you're familiar with all this. At that time there was the MUP's patron saint's day and the MUP security service's day, but this document here referring to the MUP's patron saint's day. It says here acting minister Tomislav Kovac, probably somebody from the committee drew this up. I'm not saying that this is -- there's anything wrong about this, but it was done by some committee, I'm sure. So that they made a mistake. The occasion was not Security Services Day, it was the MUP's patron saint's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what does it say in B/C/S? Could you read that phrase because my English translation says "day of security services." Could you read that line, those two lines, before the list of names. Just read it in your language and we'll hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, the names? Milos Zuban, Zoran Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, no, the two lines above the name, could you read that, please, just out loud.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I establish the organisational committee for the observing of the celebration of Security Services Day."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And number 3 on the committee is Simo Drljaca who is listed as being in the cabinet of the minister. So he was in your cabinet in November of 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand this to mean that he was a member of my office. I don't know what he may have been doing there. I don't know what's meant by this anyway because in the office of the minister there was a secretary and that was more or less it. What could Simo Drljaca possibly have done there? I cannot comment really. He was never a member of my inner management circle. Who put him here as a member of the minister's office, I really don't know, but it did happen that sometimes the cleaning lady was also listed as a member of the minister's office -- for payroll purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this document says, "I herewith establish the committee ..." and your name's the name on the bottom of the document. So you don't know -- you didn't know that Simo Drljaca was part of the cabinet of the minister? I'll withdraw the question. Let me show you another document that may help and before I go, look at the bottom. It says: "The first session of the committee is hereby scheduled for 0900 hours on 10 November 1993 in 'Kosuta' building in Jahorina. "Attendance is obligatory." Keep that in mind while we go to another document. This is tab 105, 65 ter number 20218, and I'll hand you a hard copy of that with the usher's assistance before we take the break in a few minutes. And while it's coming around, I'll tell you this document are the minutes of the expanded session of the Ministry of the Interior collegium held on the 10th and 11th of November in Jahorina and the meeting started at 1000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 105, it's at line 24 on page 49 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you were acting minister at the time, Mr. Kovac, and it says that at the session on the 10th of November -- this is after the agenda and the second paragraph -- after the agenda you find that. It says: "At the session which on 10 November Dragan Kijac presided and on 11 November the acting minister Tomo Kovac." And it lists the people who were present and Stojan Zupljanin, chief of CSB Bijeljina, is there, still the chief in November 1993 apparently. And chief of the department for public relations, Simo Drljaca. Does that refresh your memory as to what his job was in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can't help me, but it's quite possible that he was a member of the office of the chief of state security, but no way he could have been member of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he's here at the collegium, he's listed as the chief of the department for public relations. It seems to me that the minister or the ministry would have an office for public relations rather than the state security department would have an office for public relations. That's the secret police. They don't want public relations. All right, then. How about Mr. Zupljanin listed here as chief of CSB Bijeljina November 10th and 11th?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I think Mr. Zupljanin is actually listed as chief of security centres of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did I say? I'm sorry, you're right, Your Honour. I meant to say "Banja Luka" rather than "Bijeljina," and the chief of CSB Bijeljina was Petko Budisa at that time, right, a guy who used to work for you, I believe.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what he did for me. Everybody worked for me because they were members of that institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I meant he'd worked for you in Ilidza; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was commander while I was chief, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what do you have to say about this listing of Mr. Zupljanin, still as the CSB chief in November 1993? That's after the September rebellion you told us about, that's after the October 1993 document I showed you with your name listed as the minister and appointing Stojan Zupljanin to that position. You were the only one in the position to appoint Mr. Zupljanin to anything in September, October, and November 1993 because there was no minister. It was only you as the acting minister; right? Mr. Adzic was gone. There wasn't another minister yet?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. It seems that you failed to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you make it -- wait --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you make it very briefly because we're past the time for the break, so make it a short explanation and you can carry on later if you need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be allowed to answer. Mr. Hannis did not want to show the witness the list of participants and it refers to what the witness spoke about when he spoke about the commission in Pecanac, and I think that the witness should be allowed to proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, sorry, Mr. Krgovic is incorrect, Your Honour. My question was: You were the only one in the position to appoint him as a chief of the CSB in October or November of 1993. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's your answer to that? There was no minister, there was no one higher in the MUP of the RS than you in October and November of 1993; right? Yes or no, if you can.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're putting me in a position in which the only answer I can give you is that Brane Pecanac was the only one in charge of Banja Luka centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- along with this special commission. That was a factual state of affairs. I don't know how else to explain to you because we had emergency measures introduced in the area of Banja Luka. How can I explain this if you are not willing to understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. No, I'm just asking you to answer my question. Was there anyone higher than you in the MUP that could have put Mr. Zupljanin in the position of chief of CSB in October or November 1993, yes or no? I understand about the commission and we can talk about that after the break. There wasn't anybody, right? There wasn't a minister. You were the acting minister, nobody higher than you, Tomo Kovac; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emergency measures were introduced in Banja Luka directly by the president of the republic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- answered my question. My question isn't about the emergency measures of the commission. My question is about: Who was the top dog in the RS MUP in October and November 1993? That was you, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're trying to make me to speak on cross-purposes with you, and I'm really not willing to give you an answer in such circumstances in such --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a fair question and I would ask that you direct the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, unless something is being lost in the translation, what comes across to us is a question which easily admits of a yes or no answer. Mr. Hannis' question relates to a specific period in time, in October/November of 1993, and the question is simply whether you were the - to use his word - the top dog, the only person who would have been in a position to appoint the -- Mr. Zupljanin at the time. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Who was then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So who then would have been in a position to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since in the Banja Luka centre emergency measures had been imposed by the president of the republic and according to that he set up a commission to run the centre on a temporary basis, that were the consequences of the rebellion that had taken place in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we're past the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- we would take a break and resume in 20 minutes. And, Mr. Hannis, it was pointed out to me about six minutes ago that you had 15 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I confer about that because I thought -- I originally had two hours, then I was granted an additional session, which I take to be 80 minutes, and that would give me basically three hours and 20 minutes or three hours and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will return to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As the witness makes his way back in, I must apologise for the confusion in terms of time. The extended session today and the sitting until the usual time tomorrow was to accommodate the additional session that was granted to each of the -- to each side. And we have been advised in the -- so, no, that's an additional 80 minutes. And we have been advised, though, that with the -- that we can't go until 1.45. We must stop at 1.30 and then we pick up at 2.30 and then sit until 4.00. So, what that means arithmetically is, Mr. Hannis, you have, as we speak, 90 minutes left, 80 plus 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hannis, I would suggest that you try - I say "you try" because I had the experience myself - but try to prioritise so that you can get at the end of what you want to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I tried to do that -- some of that during the break. When I first heard 15 minutes, I did some prioritising. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, during the time that you were minister, just as a general proposition, when you sent out an order, did you expect it to be complied with and did you require it to be complied with?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, each and every order in the Ministry of the Interior was for the most part in the form of orders or commands, and in legal terms they were binding, provided they were issued in line with the regulations in force, so this is how the MUP operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I know it seems a fairly basic, fundamental question, but if you would issue me an order to perform some legal task under the law and the rules of the MUP and I failed to do it or refused to do it, what could happen to me? Could I be disciplined? Could I be suspended? What recourse did you have against me, who failed to follow or refused to follow your order as the minister?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the minister of the interior mainly issued orders mainly addressed to administrations, centres, stations, and units, not so much to individuals. And direct orders were then issued by lower-ranking officials, if this is what you are talking about. So the procedure was such that somebody would come up with a proposal to institute proceedings, whether in the first instance or in an appeals proceedings; and if the minister himself observed some irregularities, he himself was entitled to instruct the supervisor to institute proceedings against one of his employees. So the minister was entitled to order one of his subordinates to institute proceedings if he himself observed some infringement. Then the head of that department would then institute the proceedings. It wasn't the minister who was directly involved in that phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. And I was asking you in the context of when you were minister, was the situation the same in terms of orders being expected and being required to be followed, was that the same in 1992 when Mico Stanisic was the minister?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally speaking, yes. I can't speak about specific cases. That was the legal foundation and we had to adhere to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. And in that regard did Mr. Stanisic, to your knowledge, ever have - as minister in 1992 - ever have direct communication with an SJB chief or did he only do that through some other means, do you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to give you a professional explanation. It was possible for the minister to have direct contacts with beat policemen; that was his right. He was entitled to communicate with police stations. However, when it comes to disciplinary proceedings, the provisions are quite clear. It provides for the first-instance proceedings and the appeals proceedings. And it is the chief of the SJB or the CSB was the one to institute first-instance proceedings, and it was always conducted at that level. When it came to appeals proceedings, it was conducted at a different level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, by a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But talking outside the context of discipline, the minister could call up an SJB chief without going through the CSB chief; right? He could do that if he wanted to, in 1992? As a matter of fact, didn't Minister Stanisic have some direct communications with you when you were chief in Ilidza without going through Zoran Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about regular procedure, no; but if there was some emergency situation, we had certain contacts. For example, if the territory of my station was to be captured by enemy forces, I sought help because the situation was so serious, and due to that I had several contacts with him. And of course, later on I had other contacts in which we had direct discussions about everything and eventually about my transfer from Ilidza to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I next want to show you an order from Mr. Stanisic in late July 1992. This is tab 36 in the Prosecution binder. It's Exhibit 1D176. If the usher would assist me, I'll give you a hard copy, Mr. Kovac. I know this is dated about a week or ten days before you actually took up your new position as assistant minister. While that's coming around, let me ask you one short question. If the minister didn't have time to send a dispatch, could he issue an oral order, either face-to-face or over the phone?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if at issue were war operations or dangerous situations or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me know when you've had a chance to familiarise yourself with that order enough to tell me whether you had seen it before in 1992 or you were familiar with the general provisions of it, about reducing the components of the police and disbanding special units, removing criminals and other undesirables. Did you know about that order when you came to the ministry in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at, I probably knew of it. This is a sequence of activities that Stanisic undertook. I see that this is only a few days after I already handed over my duties at the Ilidza station, and I see that Vlasto Kusmuk was still the assistant minister and he was dismissed during that period. But these are MUP activities that Stanisic implemented during the time he was in the ministerial position. And these measures coincide with a continuation of the activities at the time when I took up the position of assistant minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We may come back to that topic, but first I now want to return to your letter of 9 August to the prime minister and the president with your recommendation about sorting out the problems of detained persons and needing to categorise them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said yesterday at transcript page 27051 that -- this was your wish to do things as quickly as possible, and I wonder, you were there only three days. How did you manage to gather the information to come up with that proposed solution? I think you said you worked with other people in the ministry, but can you recall who by name or position assisted you in collecting that information?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to be inaccurate, but I always used the word "we," and by that I meant the institution. Of course, this document was initiated by me and I stand behind it, but this is the outcome of the work of the entire organisation. If you look at the previous Stanisic's order and all the obligations contained there, just if all these obligations were complied with, would give me enough material for drafting this kind of document because good communication between the ministry, the government, and the president was crucial. At the time there were written traces left of them and they were binding for everyone involved to undertake measures or be held to account if they failed to do so. So this was the only format if you wanted to have your initiatives complied with and if you want to leave a trace behind it, an official trace. So once again I'm talking about an institution, and I often use the pronoun "we," but of course it is quite clear that I was behind each and every document of this kind and my clear intention was to put a stop to certain things. So that was a sequence of activities within the MUP. Stanisic had an opportunity to look at this all afterwards and he never had any objection. This is like a card game when you play in pairs, and once it's over you can't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that may have answered my next question which was: Did Mr. Stanisic see it before you sent it out to the president and the prime minister? And it sounds like he did not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, let us be quite clear. I don't know if he saw it or not, but this was the pattern of the division of power. If his closest associate sent a government -- sent a document to the government, this did not constitute anything irregular or part of discontinued practice. This was in conformity with the continued practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not trying to suggest any irregularity. I'm just trying to inquire whether he saw it before or only after. Now, you said at 27053 yesterday: "In a civil war, everybody thinks it's only the opposing side who committed all the crimes and that attacked the civilians, and I think this is a phenomenon that is present in every civil war. I believe that these were exactly the stages in a war that required our efforts to strengthen the ministry, the judiciary, and all other institutions in order for them to be able to wrestle with this problem." And as I understand it, the problem that you were talking about related primarily to the problem of you have these civilians, these non-combatants, because they have no place else to go, there's a war going on, they've been collected or gathered up or brought to places where they're being detained. They're not prisoners of war, they're not subject to regular criminal proceedings, and yet they're being detained for longer than three days without any charge. Is that the problem you were talking about or an aspect of the problem you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I said exactly in the words that you quoted. I never mentioned three days. I was speaking about the phenomenon itself. And whatever I said is true, I stand by it, but I would like to clarify something. We were not a separate institution within the body of Republika Srpska which were pursuing one course of action and combat, whereas there are others who are acting in a parallel or a contradictory way. According to the law and according to the hierarchy, we were the strongest structure within the state; and therefore, our legal and our ethical duty and obligation was to try and prevent these occurrences. Of course, when you have disintegration of a state, it always is coupled with the destruction of the system of values. Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina broke up as states simultaneously. An attempt to set up Bosnia-Herzegovina, Republika Srpska, and everything else that was done, including the setting up of the institutions, were certain processes. There were serious rifts, and these were difficult and painful processes. But we managed to set up the structure with the assistance of the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we don't disagree. This kind of thing happened on all sides with civilians who were sort of in the middle of the conflict. It happened to Serb civilians in Croatia or in the Muslim-held territory in Bosnia and vice versa. But I guess the point I'm driving at, this is not a surprising event. It's to be expected in the context of a civil war like that. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you have professionals and experts involved, but where did you have experts for civil war in Crisis Staffs and other bodies and particularly among ordinary people? We didn't have such experts. People acted on the basis of the so-called collective psychology, because very often people do something to other people that they fear will be done to themselves. So this is this loss of the system of value, where you have collective consciousness which acts either aggressively or whether the whole population surrender itself in order to avoid the loss of life. And these are the instances of the so-called collective amnesia that has been thoroughly studied, and that's what we had on the ground. It was difficult to resume a state of normality and an order among the ordinary people, and it's been going on for 20 years now and we are still far away from the final goal. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't have to answer the question, but I would agree with you on that. Now, what I'm trying to drive at, though, is that in August of 1992 when you wrote this letter, it could not have come as a surprise to anybody in the RS government or the police or the army, that this situation was going on. Because -- I don't recall. I know you were not at the July 11th meeting in Belgrade of the collegium because you weren't in your position yet, and I don't remember if you ever saw the minutes of that meeting, but Mr. Zupljanin spoke at that meeting and talked about the problem of the Crisis Staffs and the army trying to arrest as many Muslims as possible and bring them in and dumping them basically on the police to guard and take care of. And knowing that many of these people rounded up that way included civilians who were not combatants, not prisoners of war, not subject to criminal proceedings. So would you agree with me that it was not some sudden surprise in August, or do you not know whether it was surprising to the leadership?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, there is not a single document, and that applies to the preparations carried out by Crisis Staffs, that contains any preparations for the war to be involved with the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak more slowly. The interpreters cannot cope with this pace. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The interpreters are requesting for you to speak more slowly, Mr. Kovac. And if you could finish that shortly, I want to put another question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just that the first part of the witness's answer was not recorded properly. Either we do the verification request or the witness again gives his answer, but slowly so the interpreters can follow him. Otherwise, it's useless. There have been so many mistakes in the transcript because of the witness's pace on answers that more or less a lot of it is unusable completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, in light of that, please keep that in mind and try to speak slowly. I know I speak too quickly sometimes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we have him repeat that last answer for clarity?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, actually my question was: Do you agree with me? It could have been yes or no. Certainly if you want to hear the whole answer, I was going to propose to move on and ask then that the translation be verified for whatever it is, but it is sort of non-responsive to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, do you recall when there was an international furor of sorts of non-Serbs being held in some of the facilities in the Prijedor area like Omarska and Keraterm in early August; do you recall that? It was big news in the region, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, but I don't know why. It was the Ministry of the Interior and my enactment -- it wasn't a letter -- was the document by which the president of the republic and the government were requested to take measures. I needn't repeat which. And it referred to these very incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you want to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, let me --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our proposal was for these or such things to be eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The point I'm driving at is that before you wrote your letter on the 9th of August, there had already been events that were causing the government and the police and Ministry of Justice to be concerned about conditions in the detention facilities and the camps, and I put it to you that the reason behind that was because of all this international furor arising from the visit of reporters to Omarska and Manjaca and the publication in the media of videos and photographs of some of the prisoners in those facilities. You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That did not influence me, it didn't matter. I was trained differently and I thought along different lines. We had our own opinion and our own position about the need to eliminate these things, and I didn't worry in the least about the international community because in the two preceding months I was involved in intensive correspondence with them. That was at Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I guess I need to show you a couple documents. The first one is tab 132, this is Exhibit P1330. I'll hand you a copy, Witness. This is dated the 6th of August, the day I think you took up your duties with the ministry. It's a decision from President Karadzic. It's a very short one. It says that: "The Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Justice are obligated to obtain official written information in a co-ordinated manner on the treatment of prisoners of war by the Serb authorities and on the conditions in prisons." Were you aware of this? Did you see this when you first arrived and were working on your letter to send to the president?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you another one. Tab 133, Exhibit 179.23. I'll hand you a hard copy, with the continued assistance of the usher with my appreciation. This next one you'll see in a minute is from Prime Minister Djeric. It's a public announcement dated the 7th of August, 1992. And you'll see he says at the beginning: "In view of the CNN broadcast from 6 August concerning -- regarding the status of prisoners in Omarska, we could witness once again this network has reached a high level in producing and not reporting the news." Does that refresh your memory about there being some concern about the publicity in the international community about Omarska?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how this could jog my memory. This is a public announcement of the prime minister. We had our own ways of passing on information and analysing information. This is an ad hoc move of the political leadership, whereas we had a systematic approach. One thing is issuing ad hoc public announcements and waving them to the journalists and another thing is tackling things in a systematic matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But are you telling me you never saw those images or pictures from Omarska in early August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I did not see them, but I look at all these things through the eyes of a police officer. I didn't deal with that much because we had operatives on the ground who were duty-bound to inform us of everything they had observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These pictures may have been -- or these images may have been impressive but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were not aware of the information that police were involved in detaining and guarding of some of those persons? Looking at it as a police officer, you didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm surprised that you're putting this to me because you see that I'm one of the officials - that's clear to -- that's clear to see - who was among the first to point out irregularities in documents originating from me. I reacted to irregularities very soon, early on, and wanted to put an end to them but in a legal and a regular manner, not by means of pamphlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I commend you for that, but the point I'm trying to make to you is that it didn't get started with your initiative; it got started because there was this public international outcry and that's what got Mr. Karadzic to issue an order and start scrambling around to find out what is the story with these camps. Let me show you 1D563, which is tab 133, I believe. If the usher could help me understand again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think it's 134, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're probably right, Your Honour. Well, I may have mis-numbered them. 134 is a news article in my binder. Is that different on the list?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, this is dated the 8th of August, 1992, from Mico Stanisic as the minister to all CSBs, et cetera. And I think this is in reference to that direction or decision of President Karadzic that we looked at from the 6th of August for the Ministry of the Interior and the justice ministry to get information about treatment of war prisoners and conditions in those facilities. The second paragraph at the bottom, Mico Stanisic says: "We are stressing that the Ministry of the Interior itself is responsible for taking measures to deal with civilian population." Did you see this document? Did you know about this the day before you wrote your letter to the president and the prime minister?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look here. You said something very serious a minute ago, namely, that we initiated these measures only after an international outcry in the media. This is something that I find hurtful because only a few days earlier, I protected 300 Muslim civilians with my own body. On the other hand, I was instructed and trained by the international community because I was there rapporteur for 60 days from Ilidza. I was the rapporteur for OSCE for 50 days and I was trained as their collaborator about the ways of conduct and the ways of reporting. So I knew how -- what I was supposed to do at those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the desire to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to have an adequate and appropriate ministry in the RS. So I don't think I deserve this from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you shouldn't take offence. I'm not trying -- I'm not trying to offend you and I'm not questioning that perhaps you didn't know about those things when you wrote your proposed solutions. But I'm saying that other high-level officials were responding to a media event and that's what the timing of all this shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I think I made a mistake in citing the reference. 1D563 was not on my list. It was on, I think, Mr. Stanisic's list at tab 27. So for the record I need to note that. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Relating to prisoners, I want to ask you a question about exchanges. Were you aware of the Republic Exchange Commission in the Republika Srpska? Did you know about its existence for the exchange of prisoners and dead persons and --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you know a policeman named Slobodan Markovic? I know Markovic is a fairly common name.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely. I don't know where he's from, which part of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know a Slobodan Markovic who worked with or on the exchange commission in 1992? It doesn't look like you do.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I can't remember. I don't know where he may be from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, let me show you one last document that I'm curious about. Are you familiar with the minister ever requesting from places of detention for an individual to be released for exchange in 1992? Do you know if Mr. Stanisic ever did that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I know that Mandic did. He intervened and he wanted to exchange some people for his mother or somebody, but the ones exchanged were perpetrators of criminal offences. I'm referring to Momcilo Mandic, the then deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that happened earlier in the war, April or May, right, that event with Mr. Mandic and his mother? When you were still in Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I show you one more document? This is tab 49 in the Prosecution binder, Exhibit P1475. There were a lot of exchanges going on during 1992, not only by the official exchange commission but privately as well. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess. I was never involved in private exchanges. There was one case where Mandic requested some persons to be exchanged, and I think that -- or no, actually, I'm sure that he was successful in that. I know of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is dated the 30th of August, from Mr. Stanisic to the administration of Kula prison and the Ministry of Justice Commission for Exchange, asking to ensure the release of a prisoner Anes Bucan to be exchanged for three Serbian families and the bodies of four Serbian soldiers. Rajko Kusic, who I think was with the special police, was to organise it. Do you know anything about this, why the minister was involved with this exchange?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see that the minister was involved, only that he contacted the Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners. But it can clearly be seen from this that Anes Bucan is requested for three Serbian families and some bodies. I know that -- I know from my experience with Sarajevo that we exchanged soldiers for Serbian families in Sarajevo who were unable to move freely. One way was for them to travel by illegal channels and pay off criminals and the other way was this, and this was probably what Minister Stanisic was faced with and he requested the commission to carry out such an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to skip a couple of things here in the interest of my remaining time and ask you about -- a few questions about Dragan Andan. You knew Mr. Andan before the war, didn't you? You both had worked in state security? How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. We were never close, but I did know him as he worked in the state security, in another department, though, so we didn't work together. Later on he was a commander in a municipality while I was commander in another municipality of the city of Sarajevo. We did not work together, but we belonged to the same secretariat and security services centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think you testified that the reason that led to Andan's eventual dismissal, the specific reason was using a gambling machine or a poker machine that he'd gotten out of stores for -- allegedly to use for some police purpose, but instead used it for private purpose. But you mentioned there was a rebellion in Bijeljina by the police against Andan, is that right, before you went up there and that's why you were checking into it because the police wanted to get rid of Dragan Andan?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijeljina there was a protest of members of the reserve police mostly, and they demanded that the leadership be replaced not only Andan, but the people who ran the Bijeljina centre. But they -- they stressed the demand that Dragan Andan no longer be in a position to be in charge, and their criticism was that they were badly equipped and there were also allegations of material gain on the part of some individuals and individual or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Illegal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- disposal of some assets at the Ministry of the Interior. I proposed that he be suspended and that a procedure -- the legal procedure be initiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And we've seen in the minutes from the September 9th collegium of the MUP that Dragan Andan was to be suspended for this improper use of the gambling machine, but that's two days before the documents that we have with Mr. Stanisic's name on them initiating or requesting the initiation of disciplinary proceedings and then the actual conclusion. Did you -- you were the one who informed Mr. Andan that he was being suspended, aren't you? You did that personally, face-to-face?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that it was my duty to inform him of his suspension, but I'm sure that I did inform him that he couldn't stay in his position. Whether I told him about the suspension and whether I told him that he couldn't stay in the ministry if he continued to act that way, well, yes, I did, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the commission was set up for his suspension, and I don't see what could be -- what could be the problem with that because that was my opinion, my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The commission that investigated Mr. Andan also investigated Cedo Kljajic for a number of irregularities. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said at the outset, the protest of the police was directed against the executives, Dragan Andan, Kljajic, and others. I believe that Minister Stanisic removed them by circumventing me. There was a certain Devedlaka, if I remember as well, he and his like were all eliminated from the area of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me put a proposition to you. We have in evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would cite you to the transcript at page 21454.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- that I suggest, Mr. Kovac, that the reason there was a rebellion by the reserve police against Mr. Andan and perhaps Mr. Kljajic was because Andan and Kljajic and Mico Davidovic, in order to deal with the problem of a bloated component of reserve police, there was something like a thousand reserve police in Bijeljina, including what was described as a lot of mama's and papa's boys who didn't want to go to the front and were hiding basically in the reserve police, they came up with a ruse to trick those guys. They called them all in and they told them a false story, the false story being that there was a breakthrough about to occur on the front and he asked for volunteers who would come with Mr. Andan to fight. And about a third stepped over and volunteered, and the others he directed the police to take away their weapons and their equipment and take them over to the barracks and turn them over to the army, and that's what happened. And that's why there was such a fuss in Bijeljina, because of what had happened to those reserve policemen. Did you know about that? That's why people were upset.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this story is true. I faced those people and I don't believe that the qualification of mama's and papa's boys is true, because I spoke to some parents of killed members who complained about their sons of being sent to combat without adequate equipment. The three people mentioned plus this certain Mico Davidovic, who behaved very badly as a para group, he hailed from that area but his intentions were never honourable --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mico Davidovic was there because he had been requested by the officials in the RS, by Mr. Karadzic, by Mico Stanisic. That's why he was there. Didn't you know that? He wasn't a para group. He was from the federal MUP and he came pursuant to an official request. You didn't know that? Yes or no, please. We're near the time for our next break.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I didn't know anything about these federal structures. I was a man from Sarajevo and I was only familiar to the structures of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I neither recognised nor knew any other structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Time for our break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and we return at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm advised that you have 40 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I will do my very best to come in on time. And to save time, as the usher is passing by if he would take a document from me and hand it to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This first one is tab 26 in the Prosecution's binder, 65 ter number 20147.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, the first document I want to show you, which will be in your hand in a minute, is dated the 13th of June, 1992, from the Ilidza national security department chief Predrag Ceranic. You know him, of course?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is a report about Sinisa Milic, also known as Mongo. Have you seen this report or do you remember seeing this report in 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there's another report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There may be. This is the only one I have seen. Paragraph 2 says that --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 2 says that Mr. Milic has been known to state security. He was under operative processing. He was engaged as a collaborator of the SDB. So I take it -- I mean, he was working for some body like you mentioned in the beginning, that when you were in the SDB you had sort of hired guns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I take it he was not an employee of the state security department, but he was a contract worker for somebody who was in state security? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He worked with Zeljko Kozina who was an operative, a Croat, and Zeljko Kozina used him to disrupt inter-ethnic relations even before the war in Ilidza started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinisa took part in physical abuse committed by the so-called Serbian group from Ilidza. He used to beat up people upon orders of Zeljko Kozina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And was he -- was he, in 1992, ever associated with Brne Gavrilovic's group, Brne's Chetniks, do you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. He worked mostly on his own, and I had information that he was maintaining contacts with the SDB of the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you'll see three paragraphs above Mr. Ceranic's name and signature that it says Milic is a drug addict. He's been creating numerous and big problems. For example, yesterday, on 12 June, he shot dead 22 Muslims. He'd gone to Vogosca to take them over and then he killed them. And the aggravating factor was that this caused political damage because UNPROFOR men witnessed the incident. So you knew about that back in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if you look at this paragraph there, in addition to this, each group that came to Ilidza, like Arkan's or Seseljevci --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Milic would try to persuade them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You answered my question. I've only got 35 minutes left. I have to be --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the Defence will have time to follow-up on these things when they have their turn, if they want. But my question was if you knew about it back in June of 1992 and you said yes. Was he ever arrested?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he ever arrested for that crime? Was he ever arrested for that crime?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an individual who tried to assassinate me. Why are you asking me about his arrest? He tried to kill me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he arrested for trying to assassinate you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it's clearly stated here -- there was no time. He died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I want to take you then to a collegium meeting on the 3rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is tab 60, Your Honours. And with the usher's help, if I could hand a hard copy to Mr. Kovac. It's 1D510. This is a collegium on 3rd of October in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kovac, I really only have one question for you regarding -- one or two questions for this one. You're listed as being in attendance. Do you remember this collegium meeting on 3 October 1992?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly, but as I'm looking at the minutes I'm reminded of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. If you would look at your page 2 at the bottom, under the second paragraph, under item number 4, it says: "Tomislav Kovac briefed the Advisory Board on the security situation in the territory of Bijeljina ..." Do you remember giving the group a briefing on the security situation in Bijeljina at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since it's recording in the meeting -- minutes of the meeting, I may have just said something briefly. I don't think that I provided an extensive report at this kind of collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember advising the group that about eight days before, in Bijeljina, three Muslim families, a total of 25 persons from the Malagic, Sejmenovic and Sarajlic families had been murdered in Bijeljina? Did you tell them about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you did know about it on October 2003, didn't you, because it had been in the local media?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the sense that I knew of it officially. I didn't have any official report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it then you had some sort of unofficial report or information about it, and as a policeman, didn't you have an interest in following up on the murder of 25 people, including women and children?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any information about 25 people being killed. There were some accusations on Radio Bijeljina and certain services were tasked to investigate this within the regular scope of their work. I think that at that time all the other organs became involved, but this was not my area. This was the area of the security services centre and the district prosecutor's office. But specifically because at that time I didn't have any information about any families being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you now to the next collegium meeting on the 5th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the usher could assist. It's Exhibit P1270. Thank you. This one was also held in Bijeljina. The tab number is 74.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you're listed among the attendees of this meeting. Let me tell you what I'm specifically interested in in this one, on the first page it mentions the minister chaired the meeting until the third item of the agenda when he had to leave. And then Under-Secretary Cedo Kljajic took over. And on the bottom of your page 1 and on to page 2 of the English, it mentions that Mr. Kusmuk, Mr. Karisik, and Rade Radovic had attended the meeting but they also were excused due to problems which emerged in Zvornik. Do you know that the minister went to Zvornik from this meeting because of some problem that had arisen between the special police and the military police in Zvornik? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at the moment that that was the reason for his visit, but I am aware of the problems that occurred between the special police and some elements of the military police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you a couple other documents related to that one. This is tab 76. It's 65 ter 30033. And with the usher's help I'll hand you a copy of the hard copy. While it's on its way, Mr. Kovac, I'll tell you it's a regular combat report from the Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade, and item number 4 is about extraordinary events. It says: "... as previously reported, a serious clash between the military police and a Republika Srpska Special Unit is still taking place. It is being kept under control and likely to be resolved favourably without consequences. In the course of the day, General ... Gvero and the minister of internal affairs visited Zvornik Garrison." Did you have any conversation with Mr. Stanisic about this conflict or his visit on 5 November to deal with it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having spoken to him, but I think that later on I think I talked to Karisik who was an official there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was anybody disciplined in either the special unit or the military police concerning that event?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I'm not aware of any proceedings instituted due to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before I forget, I had showed the witness the 13 June report from Ilidza concerning Mongo. I'd like to tender that document. He's identified Mr. Ceranic and talked about the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Exhibit P2459, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies to the Registry. I think I may have cut you off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So my question was to have the tab number for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it. I think that was tab number -- tab number 26, I believe, Your Honour. Do you find it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, concerning those murders of the Muslim families in Bijeljina, I'd like to show you Exhibit Number -- 65 ter 30035. It's tab 116. This is a document you will have seen before. This is a record of taking of statement from persons - in this case the person is you - it was taken on or it's recorded on the 13th of April, 2005, and I believe this was done in Zvornik. And do you remember having given this statement?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is in relation to a criminal investigation that was being done concerning those September 1992 murders; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is that I stand by this statement that I made to the authorised officials, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. It's correct and true and you don't have any changes to make?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to change anything. It is as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a couple more topics, Mr. Kovac, and then we'll be done. I want to talk about Mr. Koroman briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can show the witness 65 ter 10373, tab 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The document under tab 116, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- previous one, is not exhibited. That's right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour. It just had a 65 ter number. But I would like to tender it now that the witness has identified and confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we do object, Your Honours. First of all, a number of these documents - and we intended to raise this issue after the witness is excused - there is a number of documents that has been disclosed to us in the last two weeks, a number of Rule 68 material which was never shown to us. It was shown -- it was disclosed to us the day -- in the 11th hour, the day before the witness arrived. Some of these documents we've seen like -- yesterday in the evening for the first time they were disclosed to us. They're not on the Rule 65 ter list and I don't see any basis how Mr. Tom Hannis can offer these documents to be admitted at this point. They have closed their case. We have the procedure in this -- in this case from the very outset how the amendment to the Rule 65 ter list has to be made, with the leave of the Trial Chamber, and then offered to the -- and it has to be in writing if I correctly remember the Rules. And only then can the document be offered for admittance into the record. On this -- in this case, all this is without the merit because the documents have not been disclosed to us properly in the course of this trial. They are disclosed right now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, we're talking about one document. That should be addressed specifically than this blanket claim about having received a bunch of documents that were Rule 68. This guy, this witness, Mr. Kovac, was not a witness on the Prosecution's list. I'm not sure how Mr. Zecevic reads this document as being Rule 68 for his client --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We couldn't have known that -- he wasn't called by the Defence as a witness either. It was only when the Trial Chamber called him as a witness that it became pertinent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I'm sorry if perhaps I wasn't -- I wasn't clear enough. I was making a general observation of the situation that we are faced with in the last week or so. That goes for the Rule 68 and the newest disclosure. However, in this case, in this particular document, the witness is a viva voce witness. If Mr. Hannis wants to raise an issue from his statement, he should do so and we will have it on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, putting aside your general complaint about disclosure - which we may or may not have to come to - in dealing with this particular document haven't we previously dealt with the matter of documents which come up for the first time in cross-examination? Because this is -- this is not a -- the present witness is not a witness called by the Prosecution; it's one of the Chamber witnesses. And like yourselves, Mr. Hannis is cross-examining. So wouldn't that rule about the inapplicability of the necessity of documents having to come in by way of having been first entered on the Rule 65 ter list apply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, but the -- in this specific case it is not the cross-examination of the witness. My understanding would be, with all due respect, as yours, Your Honour, if this was an issue of the credibility of the witness. In this case, Mr. Hannis is trying to further his case, which he closed a year ago, through the Chamber's witness with the documents he failed to put on his 65 ter lists, he failed or the Office of the Prosecutor failed to tender those documents during their case. Now, at the minute to 12.00 with the very last Chamber witness, he's furthering their case by presenting some additional documents, tendering some additional documents, through this witness. It is not the issue of the credibility of the witness. It is in this specific case, it is for the purpose of furtherance of the OTP case. And I -- we -- with all due respect, I don't think that this is a proper moment to -- that we exercise in such a -- that we undertake these exercises when it comes with the -- with the testimony of -- testimonies of the Chamber's witnesses. Perhaps -- I stand, of course, in your power, Your Honours. But that is my opinion at the top of my head. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is not persuaded on -- on the -- that the objection raised by Mr. Zecevic has any basis because the nature of the -- it would have been impossible for either side to anticipate months - in some cases years - ago that the Chamber may have been calling a witness which they themselves, which either side did not at the time, consider necessary, and therefore the issue of entering a relevant statement on the 65 ter list would not have arisen. And to the extent that either side uses the -- takes advantage of the presence of a witness called by the Chamber to supplement its case is to be expected. That is the advantage which the Chamber, having called witnesses, affords to each side. And -- however, in terms of the particular document which the Prosecution wishes to now tender through this witness, subject to the Prosecution being able to identify the relevant parts of the statement in question, which, if memory serves, was a statement that the investigating authorities in, was it, Zvornik, the Chamber by a majority, myself dissenting, would agree to its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Do you need me to elaborate what portions I think are relevant? It's a very -- it's a short statement. It primarily has to do with this witness's knowledge of Dusko Malovic and his group and under whose authority they were, which has been a contested issue throughout case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, the disadvantage that we have is that we don't have it immediately up before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll move on because I think my clock is ticking. No, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So with myself dissenting, the document is admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 30035 will become Exhibit P2460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, you have that January 11, 1993, document from Mr. Njegus in your hand? I don't remember where we left off -- yeah, that's it on the --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Can you please -- I see you're very skilful in placing documents before my nose. I would like to ask you not to do that. The document that I do have in front of me is of the 1st of April, 1992, and on the other side of it is the 11th of -- some month 1993. I would like Your Honours to be spared from being toyed by the Prosecutor. I am trying to co-operate. I'm willing to do that. Maybe I cannot read documents well. I'm not sure about the date. In this document I have two dates on one sheet of paper. Can you please make sure that you do not manipulate documents in such a way. 1st of April, 1992, one document; the other date is 11th of January, 1993, on the same sheet of paper. I don't know whether this is normal here, where you can have two documents on one sheet of paper. Please, can you explain in relation to which document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might intervene. I don't know that it's necessary for the Chamber to come to counsel's Defence. But, Mr. Kovac, as would have been pointed out to you at several stages. In order from -- apart from the discrete issues which you were invited to assist the Chamber on, the method of counsel's question and the witness's answer is to aid the smooth flow of the receipt of evidence by the Chamber. And I can assure you that if counsel abuses his position as counsel, we would bring that to his attention. So unless and until there's an intervention by the Chamber, with or without the prompting of counsel from the other side, there is nothing improper in the way that counsel -- the Prosecutor in this case is proceeding. So if you would listen to the question and then give a short answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, with all this, I lost track of the tab number. Could you remind us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's tab 91.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I assure you I'm not trying to manipulate you in that fashion. I think what you have is some documents have been copied on two sides. I have the 11 January 1993 document with a blank side on the back. If you would prefer I can give that to you. But I'm only talking about the side that talks about 11 January 1993, which is apparently the decision -- or it says: "Please find enclosed the decision to assign Malko Koroman to the administration for police tasks and duties." Did you know about that in 1993, that Mr. Koroman the former SJB chief in Pale was being assigned to the administration for police tasks? Did you know?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can somebody please explain what this decision that's on the same sheet of paper dated 11th of April -- or 1st of April, 1992. Is this in any way related? This is what I'm asking you about. I have documents on both sides --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Koroman. I don't read B/C/S very well and I don't know what that is, and it's not my job to answer your questions here today. So did you know about Mr. Koroman being appointed to the administration for police tasks and affairs in January of 1993? It doesn't do you any good to look at that side. That's not the one I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, would it perhaps assist when you give the witness a document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, please. You give the witness the document with the blank other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kovac, Mr. Kovac, please, in order to save paper we have taken the habit of for copying purposes to print on both sides. So this is why you have one sheet of paper with a decision on each side. This is not an original; it is a copy. So please bear with that and move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of that. I somehow seem to lack trust, but I do have the document clearly before me. This document says: "Please find enclosed the decision to assign Malko Koroman to your administration ..." Yes, I did know about that. I knew that he was assigned to the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the position you held in January 1993, did you have any input or say so about that appointment?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. At the time the minister was Mr. Adzic and at the time I did not have any influence on the personnel policy, not even within my administration. I simply was not one of the associates that Ratko Adzic would listen to. We were in a kind of a conflict and that was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now let me show you another document and I take the risk, it's a two-sided document. It's actually two separate documents but I want to ask you about both of them in sequence. So if you'll please bear with me. If the usher would hand you this. This is also from the same tab number, it's just a different ERN. The B/C/S page is 03240402 and 0403. These documents were received from the Republika Srpska as part of a request for personnel documents so they all came together in one batch, I believe. Mr. Kovac, this will be two separate documents. And the first one is dated 18 January 1994 and I'll ask you about that one first, and the other side is a document dated 27 May 1994 and we'll talk about both of them briefly. Do you have 18 January 1994 on top? This is a decision by Minister Mico Stanisic assigning Malko Koroman to the task of chief of the department for police duties in the Sarajevo security services centre. Right. And if you want to look at the next page, it's the 27th of May, 1994, it's another decision by Mico Stanisic regarding Malko Koroman and assigning him to the duty of chief inspector for police special operations in the office of the minister. Did you know about those appointments by Mr. Stanisic in 1994 concerning Malko Koroman?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know about this chief inspector assignment and I cannot remember the other one, but I believe it must have been so. I want to believe that the documents are correct. Malko was often appointed to different positions, so most probably this is correct. What we see in the document must have been so. I do remember that he was assigned to the position of inspector for special purposes unit, so I don't recall the other appointment but it must have been so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And one other document from this series I'd like to show you, if I could get help from the usher. The ERN for this one is 03240408 -- no, I'm sorry, 0392. This is dated the 20th of October, 1995, Mr. Kovac. And this is a decision on early promotion to a higher rank. Promoting Malko Koroman from the rank of major to the -- an early promotion to the rank of colonel. And it appears to be signed by you as the minister. Do you remember promoting Malko Koroman in 1995?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I most probably did. I have no recollection at the moment of these promotions because these were not my main functions, but I do see my signature. So yes, I must have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry. I would like to tender those documents, Your Honour, but there are other documents concerning personnel status. I don't care about having those in. I don't know if the Defence wants them in because it may have something they want. Otherwise, we can take it out of e-court and put in only the ones that he's been shown and talked about specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To what end, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd rather not make that submission in front of the witness. He understands more English than I do B/C/S, if I can do that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would hold over your application until the witness is released.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
