utterances.text: And now may I inquire how many minutes I have left? I want to do my last topic and I have, I think, four documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could please any unnecessary microphone be switched off. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We think you have just sufficient time to deal with your four documents in 15 minutes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, in one of your interviews with the OTP I think in August -- yes, August 10 and 11, 2010, you met with Paul Grady, Julian Nicholls and Patrick Hayden. And during that interview, at one point they were giving you a hard time a bit about Simo Drljaca and wondering why he had not been punished because of the suspicion that he had not performed very well in connection with investigating or prosecuting people from his SJB in connection with the Koricanske Stijene murders. Do you remember that? Just in general, you remember having a conversation with Mr. Grady, Nicholls, and Hayden?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have a document to that effect? Can you show it to me? I do remember that we talked about it in general but not any details. I don't know what you wanted to ask me about. It was a long conversation. They put a lot of questions to me so --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a difficulty. I have an English transcript of that interview but that's one that I don't have a B/C/S transcript for. I think all we have is the audio. And I understand you were given a CD of it, but I don't have the time to try and find the audio and find the exact place on the audio where this was said. But let me read you what's said here and then I'll ask you if you remember saying this and then we'll go from there. It -- you're reported to have said -- let me find the exact page reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a tab number and reference, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, this interview was tab number 3 on the Trial Chamber's list, and in the English transcript it's at page 76, line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in response to this hard time you said: "It's important that you look at the causes and the movement of everything to see where we got at the end because Simo Drljaca was not created by Serb MUP. Simo Drljaca and many like him were placed on the basis of negative selection, what I call -- and compromises between the SDA, SDS, and HDZ. And Simo Drljaca's decision on appointment for the chief of the station in Prijedor was signed by Alija Delimustafic and his assistant, Selimovic. They appointed" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Hannis. May I remind you that the -- what you're saying has to be interpreted so perhaps you need to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm on my last two short sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Signed by Alija Delimustafic and his assistant, Selimovic. They appointed him and they got what they got." Do you remember saying that? Or if not, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember talking about what the results were on the basis of appointments that were made as a part of the distribution of power between the three parties. Many of the personnel were not appointed on the basis of their quality, but because they wanted to have their people at certain positions. Through such processes, we got some of the personnel and I believed that Simo Drljaca was - at least that was my view at the time - I believe that Simo Drljaca was one of such personnel members. I did specify some other people. When I speak about these people, I speak about people who were appointed or proposed for the positions by the Crisis Staffs, the SDS, SDA, and so on, Municipal Boards, and that's how the things worked at the time, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, do you know, Mr. Drljaca was never appointed by Alija Delimustafic because Mr. Drljaca didn't become an SJB chief until mid-April 1992, after the war had already started. Did you know that? He couldn't have been appointed by Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that, but at that moment I was thinking of Crisis Staffs, so it must have been the Crisis Staff. Given their political power, it must have been them who in fact - not officially but in fact - appointed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you're right about that. But let me show you now tab number 135. This is Exhibit 65 ter 30046. I'll give you a hard copy. While it's on its way, Mr. Kovac, I'll tell you it's dated the 30th of July, 1992, as you may see on the screen. It's a decision appointing Simo Drljaca as chief for Prijedor Public Security Station by Stojan Zupljanin. And I note the first paragraph makes reference to this decision being pursuant to the Law on State Administration, a decision of the minister of 25 April 1992, and with prior approval from the minister of the interior. I take it you've never seen this before? But do you have any reason to doubt the authenticity of that document, which appears to be from Banja Luka by Stojan Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This clearly shows the illegality of this decision because it should have been taken by the minister with the approval of the centre chief. It is very clear that such a decision was not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Because this is by the centre chief, Stojan Zupljanin, and it says within it it's with the prior approval of the minister. So it appears it has been done in compliance with the law; right?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I'm sorry. But these are things that I do know about. This is a flagrant contravention of the law, and the law was very clear on this. The Banja Luka centre cannot appoint a --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- public security station chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre chief is below the minister in the hierarchy and not the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please, this is at least for the third time. Whenever -- I must say, it appears almost that whenever you don't like the answer, you are cutting the answer of the witness in half.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So please -- well, that is my impression. I'm sorry and I do apologise if I'm getting the wrong impression but that is what I -- I was tend to -- for some reason, I have that impression. Perhaps I'm wrong and I do apologise. But in any case, the witness should be allowed to finish his statement, his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears to have been done in compliance with the law; right? No, sir. That's an answer. If there's a further explanation, I can ask for it or you can ask for it on your turn. I'm sorry. I apologise, Your Honours, I shouldn't be talking directly to counsel. I apologise, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kovac, you don't know what that 25 April decision, 1992, says, do you? That was a decision by the minister specifically delegating his authority to the centre chiefs to appoint SJB chiefs. Do you see the reference to a 25 April 1992 decision, number 01-25/92? You're not familiar with that document, are you?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with it, but this decision shows me how Drljaca rose to power, and if we were to continue to analyse this, we would probably come up with the conclusion that the centre chief didn't have much say in this either. To my mind, this is illegal. I have never seen anything like it before and this is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but I think there's something wrong in translation or in transcript, rather, because -- can the witness repeat that because what is recorded is not what the witness said. Witness said the chief of CSB didn't have anything with that or didn't have too much influence on that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If it's a question of a misunderstanding or mistranslation, perhaps the witness can repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It is good now. It is corrected, Your Honour. I saw after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just a couple more documents, I hope, Mr. Kovac. If we could look at 0 -- I'm sorry, this is -- this is 65 ter 30043 -- or -- yes. And this will be tab number 129. And I want one particular page out of it now which is 03240291, dated 17 January 1994. I don't know if you can see it on the screen, but it is from Minister Mico Stanisic, 17 January 1994, a decision temporarily assigning Simo Drljaca as assistant chief of the Banja Luka security services centre. Did you know about that appointment by Mr. Stanisic in January 1994?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but if it bears his signature than he probably carried it out. He probably tactically shifted him around, I suppose to keep him away from operative management.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know earlier you told us that you talked about this rotation of staff to keep some of these guys from thwarting investigations. But sending Mr. Drljaca, who was suspected in connection with misconduct, at least, connected to the Koricanske Stijene case, sending him to Banja Luka as deputy chief doesn't seem to be a very good place to put him, is it?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not being precise. This is assistant centre chief, but I think he was assistant chief without specific tasks. I don't know if he really had any work at the time. That's when you give a decision to somebody without any duties, to remove him, to put him on ice. And this -- but this man had stronger political support than all the rest of us together; that must have been why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And two more pages to look at. 20 October 1995, which -- I'm sorry, I'm having trouble with these double-sided pages. Again, the ERN in B/C/S is for a document in which Mr. Drljaca is being appointed or being promoted exceptionally from the rank of major to the rank of colonel by Tomo Kovac. Do you remember making that promotion?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I may have, I may not have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And finally 03240287, which is dated the 7th of October, 1994, if you help me with this one. I think this is a different minister. And do you recognise which minister that is?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here, Zivko Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he's appointing Mr. Drljaca to the position of the chief of Prijedor CJB; correct?

utterances.speaker: TOMISLAV KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have nothing further. Again, with this personnel package I'd like to call out the ones we've shown him and he's talked about and submit that later on once we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, I assume that the Defence have decided how they're going to -- who's going first and how they've divided up their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but -- I sincerely believe that it would be better if we start in the morning because I understood that Mr. Hannis was to make the submission on the documents he proposed to tender after the witness is excused. We have 15 minutes and I think that would be ample time for that, and that will of course help us to streamline our cross-examination. And I can assure the Trial Chamber that until the last session I didn't have any cross-examination for this witness. So perhaps I'm going to be fairly shorter than the time allocated to me, and my understanding is that Mr. Krgovic also will have a short cross-examination of this witness. So we can assure the Trial Chamber that in any case we will finish fairly early tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sure the witness will be relieved to hear that. Mr. Kovac, as you would have gathered from what has just passed between the Bench and counsel, there is certain procedural matters with which we have to deal with before we rise for this afternoon. But because they would not concern you, we would invite the usher to escort you outside now while we continue our other work and we will pick up with your cross-examination by counsel for the Defence tomorrow morning. And as we come to the end of a day, I remind you, as I did yesterday, that you can't discuss your testimony with anyone. You cannot communicate with counsel from the other side and your communication with your own lawyer is limited to the matter of anything that would -- might touch on the possibility of your self-incrimination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I got a little befuddled at the end because of some of the two-sided copies and not being able to find what I was looking for, but Your Honour will understand my problem. I was supposed to make a submission, but I understand that the Trial Chamber had ruled two-to-one to admit the document so I don't know if you need me to make a further submission at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, we dealt with that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It was another document where the question was relevance --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and you indicated that you couldn't -- you would wish to address in the absence of the witness. I can't remember what the document is but -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Koroman. About Koroman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's about Koroman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The promotion of Koroman or his position in the administration as an inspector, it's part of our argument, Your Honour, that certain of these individuals, Mr. Koroman, Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Drljaca, others for whom the MUP had information that they had committed disciplinary violations at least, if not criminal matters that they should be prosecuted for, instead of being disciplined or suspended or prosecuted, they were actually, some views, moved sideways or promoted. And that goes contrary to the argument that: We were trying to do something to remove the bad eggs, and therefore we think it's relevant to that issue, the failure to punish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we do object, of course, as you can imagine because -- let me give the reasons why. We know that this is the Prosecutor's case. However, the issue of Malko Koroman has been dealt with with a number of witnesses - I don't remember at this point how many - from Pale. Then we had witnesses from the MUP, the ones who were working in the personnel administration. Then we had in our case we brought Mr. Tusevljak, who was from the CSB Sarajevo, therefore directly superior to Mr. Koroman. Now, in all these cases, in all these available points, the Office of the Prosecutor chose not to present this document to these witnesses, ask their comment, and then offer these documents at the -- as exhibits. Now, if they will be permitted to do at this point such a thing, then it practically leaves us, the Defence, without the possibility to remedy that. Because had we known that this document is a part of the Prosecutor's case or had we known that this document was shown to the witness, we would have called, perhaps we would have called, the evidence to counter that or to explain these documents and why it was taken. Now, if we are -- if we are brought at this point to this position, then there would be no other remedy but to ask that we re-open our Defence case and bring some witnesses and then explain this because that -- I don't see any -- because I can't explain these documents with this witness because this witness can only say: Yes, I'm aware of the fact that this person was promoted in 1995. We have a very strict -- all this -- during the whole trial it was insistence, insistence on the time and the geography of this case. The case is -- alleges the crimes committed between 1992 April and 31st December. Now we are expanding the case by bringing the documents from 1995 in order to explain the state of mind of our client at the 11th hour. And that is why I say this, in my opinion, goes to the fairness of these proceedings and therefore we -- if your trial -- if the Trial Chamber would admit these documents at this point, we would have, unfortunately, no other way but to ask that we be allowed to re-open our case and call these witnesses and explain this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the -- what struck me as well was the dates, and that is why I asked Mr. Hannis to what end. But the -- I will ask him to respond to the specific point you made about having not taken the opportunity of having these documents tendered through some witness while their case was still open. But after the application was made, the -- perhaps an -- let me say parenthetically that I am by no means anticipating what final conclusion I might reach on this question. But the - to my mind - somewhat helpful answer which the witness also gave, that any suggestion which the Prosecution may wish to make based on what these documents say on the face of it, is not the only conclusion that's possible because not every promotion is a promotion. And it is something that you may have the opportunity to explore further in cross-examination. But let me hear Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Why weren't these tendered previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, for example, if I tried to show a document signed by Tomo Kovac or Mico Stanisic from 1994 or 1995, I might have had an objection from the Defence that, well, they need to tender it through another witness, Mr. Kovac or Mr. Stanisic. That's the kind of objection we ran into during the case on more than one occasion. Secondly, Your Honour, with regard to the 1995 document signed by Kovac, they also go to his credibility as a witness because he's told you that when he was the assistant minister and when he was head of the police administration and when he started in the ministry, part of his task was to remove those people who weren't good decision-makers or who were engaged in bad conduct. Well, he had opportunities to do something about those people and not only did he not do anything, he promoted them, early promotion, or gave them a better job or an equal job. With regard to 1994, it's Mr. Stanisic in his second term as minister having another opportunity to do something regarding people he didn't have time to do anything about in 1992 and not doing anything that appears to be in the nature of a punishment or a reprimand or a discipline. That's why these documents are being tendered. And absent of showing a prejudice, which I've heard the argument, but just because it hurts doesn't mean it's unfair prejudice that needs a remedy. It's just something that needs to be dealt with. Cross-examining this witness is one way to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the documents are admitted and marked, and we would point out for the benefit of the Defence, who have yet to begin their cross-examination of this witness, that the stage that we are at is that this is something they are able to fully explore with the witness who appears best able to answer the issues surrounding these promotions or lateral transfers, as they may have been. So --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
